messages.subject: [R-sig-ME] One last place available: Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) in R
messages.subject_clean: One last place available: Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) in R
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
 
We have one final place available on our upcoming course: Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) in R

Dates: Online, 21?24 September 


 
Course website: [ https://www.physalia-courses.org/courses-workshops/glmms-in-r/ ]( https://www.physalia-courses.org/courses-workshops/glmms-in-r/ ) 
 
 
This four-day course is aimed at graduate students and researchers with experience using generalized linear models in R who would like to develop their skills in applying mixed models to experimental and observational data.
 
The course will cover:
Specifying, interpreting and validating GLMMs
Random effects, variance structures and correlation structures
Model selection and model choice
Working with lme4 and glmmTMB
Visualising fitted models and checking model assumptions with DHARMa
Spatial, temporal and phylogenetic correlation structures
 
If you are interested in joining us, this is the last available place, so please register soon!
 
 
Best,
Carlo
 
 

--------------------

Carlo Pecoraro, Ph.D


Physalia-courses DIRECTOR

messages.subject: [R-sig-ME] glmmTMB large dataset: NaN at starting parameter values
messages.subject_clean: glmmTMB large dataset: NaN at starting parameter values
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

My name is Anabeel Sen. I?m a PhD candidate in Epidemiology at Virginia
Commonwealth University, and I?m working on a longitudinal analysis of
diabetes-related emergency department(ED) visits for my dissertation. I?m
running into a problem with glmmTMB that I haven?t been able to figure out.
Thanks Dr. Bolker for pointing me towards this list!

My dataset has about 5.1 million person-year observations, 860,000
individuals in 904 ZCTAs (Zip Code Tabulation Areas which are similar to
Zip Codes). The outcome is the annual number of diabetes-related ED visits,
and I?m using a negative binomial model with the nbinom2 family.

My original model had random intercepts for both person and ZCTA which
might have been too complex:

ed_visit_cnt ~ fixed_effects + (1 | person_id) + (1 | zcta)

My initial idea was to account for repeated observations within people and
clustering by ZCTA, while including individual-level demographic and
clinical variables and ZCTA-level social determinants of health variables.
When I ran these models on a subset of 5,000 people in 605 ZCTAs, they
converged. However, the two-random-effect model has been difficult to fit
on the full dataset. I have tried it both on my PC RStudio and my university's
high performance research computing core RStudio interface. On the R studio
interface, it tends to run for several hours at a time and then restart on
its own. I have then switched back to my PC R studio and started
simplifying the model to figure out where the problem was coming from.

When I removed all my fixed effects and the ZCTA level random effect, the
following model fits on my full dataset:

ed_visit_cnt ~ 1 + (1 | person_id) where it converges with a
positive-definite Hessian.

But when I add just one fixed effect for my year variable, it fails even
before I can start adding any of my other covariates or exposure variables

ed_visit_cnt ~ year + (1 | person_id)

The error that shows up is:

*"Negative log-likelihood is NaN at starting parameter values"*

I tried the same simplified model : (ed_visit_cnt ~ year + (1 | person_id) on
smaller subsets of the data. With approximately 50,000, 200,000, and
400,000 individuals, the models all fit successfully. The estimated year
effect was also fairly stable across those subsets as well. So I wasn't
sure if I?m running into a numerical or computational limitation related to
the combination of this many observations and huge random-effect levels.

A few questions I could pick everyone's brain and experience on include:

   -

   Is this likely a numerical/memory limitation at this scale?
   -

   Is there anything specific I could try in glmmTMB for a random-intercept
   model with this many groups?
   -

   Does the fact that the intercept-only model works, but adding year
   causes the starting likelihood to become NaN, point toward a specific issue?
   -

   Is there a limit on the number of random-effect levels that glmmTMB can
   normally handle, even if there is only a random intercept?
   -

   If this is simply too large for glmmTMB, what could be a reasonable
   alternative for accounting for repeated observations within individuals?

I would be happy to provide my exact script or a smaller reproducible
example if that would help. Any insight or suggestions would be greatly
appreciated.

With regards,
Anabeel Sen, MBBS, MPH (he/him)
Ph.D Candidate and Graduate Research Assistant
Department of Epidemiology, School of Public Health
Virginia Commonwealth University
551-777-1559 (p) - LinkedIn <https://www.linkedin.com/in/anabeelsen/>

messages.body_plain:
*Very* quick question/suggestion: is year a numeric variable (e.g.
2020, 2021, 2022) ... ? If so, you might be able to solve the problem by
centering the year variable, or doing anything to make the zero value
closer to the body of the data (i.e. you could use `year-min_year` or
`year-min_year+1`, rather than `year-mean_year`, should perform about the
same). If you're already doing that, or if centering doesn't help, a
minimal reproducible example would be useful ...
